dataset.name: SPRUCE Methane Transport in Plants at S1 Bog, Marcell Experimental Forest, Minnesota, 2017-2019
description: This data set contains measurements of methane (CH4) transport by plants (both ground-layer and trees) and diffusion, as well as whole-plot emissions, taken in September 2018 and June 2019 in S1 Bog outside of the SPRUCE (Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments) experimental enclosures. Additionally, CH4 and carbon dioxide (CO2) stable isotope data in porewater and atmospheric emissions were taken in July 2017 in the SPRUCE enclosures to explore the relative magnitude of CH4 oxidation. Episodic ebullition rates for S1 Bog are taken from Gill et al. (2017).

Methane transport is an important component of many ecosystem models of peatlands. The results were compared to two methane models that have been developed for the SPRUCE project, ELM-SPRUCE (Earth Land Model) and TECO_SPRUCE (Terrestrial ECOsystem model).

This dataset contains six data files in comma separate (.csv) format. Additional metadata are provided: six data dictionaries and a file-level metadata file in comma separate (.csv) format and a user guide in PDF (*.pdf) format.

measurementTechnique:
Study Site
Observations occurred at The Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s SPRUCE (Spruce and Peatland Responses Under Changing Environments) project (Hanson et al., 2017) at S1 bog at the U.S. Forest Service’s Marcell Experimental Forest, in Minnesota, USA (47°30.476’ N; 93°27.162’ W). SPRUCE is an ecosystem-scale study that warms the vegetation and peatland soil profile to a depth of 2 m within 12.8-m diameter open-top enclosures. The peat was heated first at – 2 m for a period of 1 year starting in summer 2014 (deep peat heating phase), then heating of the overlying air began in August 2015 starting the whole ecosystem warming phase of the experiment.

Methods
Methods are described below, for a more detailed methodology, please see:
Bridgham, S.D., J.R. White, R.M. Wilson, J.K. Keller, and J.P. Chanton. 2025. Methane transport pathways and oxidation in a Minnesota Bog. Journal of Geophysical Research – Biogeosciences: in revision.

Whole-Plot Gas Emissions (Chamber_fluxes.csv)
Gas emissions were measured with a closed, continuous-flow system in eight 0.12 m2 plots placed along the three main boardwalks (T1-T3). Plots were delineated by 39.5 cm diameter PVC chamber bases for gas measurements. Two plots were placed to intentionally capture E. vaginatum clumps, an important plant in the bog. Chamber bases were placed ~ 20 cm into the peat surface at least several days before collecting observations.
Gas emission measurements were made with portable Gasmet DX4040 Fourier-Transform Infrared (FTIR) gas analyzer (Vantaa, Finland) or a Picarro G2201-i Cavity Ring-Down Spectrometer (Santa Clara, CA, USA) in a flow-through configuration. The Picarro instrument also allowed us to measure the stable isotope signatures of CH4 and CO2 (see below). Gas samples were logged at ~ 1 hz for the Picarro G2201-i Cavity Ring-Down Spectrometer and averaged every 30 sec for the Gasmet DX4040 Fourier-Transform Infrared (FTIR) gas analyzer. The most linear portions of the regression were selected for rate calculations yielding mean CH4 r2 = 0.99 and minimum r2 = 0.94. Air volume in peat not occupied by solid matter or water was included in headspace estimates for flux calculations (increasing CH4 emissions by 20.5% on average compared to estimates that just included the headspace above the peat surface).

Ground-Layer Plant Gas Emissions (plant_fluxes.csv; plant_metrics.csv)
CH4 and CO2 fluxes and stable isotope signatures from 12 ground-layer plant species using a Picarro G2201-i. An airtight seal was created by placing polyethylene sleeves over stems or leaves of target plants, covering the entire structure to just above the peat surface and connecting the sleeve to the Picarro instrument. This typically included the entire plant of M. trifolium (the only dominant forb in S1 Bog) and of many shrubs, but for tussock-forming graminoids such as E. vaginatum only a portion of the plant was enclosed in the sleeve. Gas emissions were collected for approximately eight minutes. The most linear portions of the regression were selected for rate calculations, typically yielding r2 > 0.90, except at low emission rates. To scale up to plant-mediated CH4 fluxes from fluxes per stem or leaf, the total number of stems or leaves of each plant species in the chamber footprint were counted along with maximum leaf length for graminoids and basal stem diameter and stem length for shrub species.

Tree Gas Emissions (tree_fluxes.csv)
For tree gas emissions, chambers were made from closed-cell foam glued to an acrylic sheet around the stem (Pitz et al., 2018). Emissions were measured once on each tree stem randomly from 16 to 180 cm from the peat surface. Measurements were made using a Picarro G2201-I in a similar manner to the plant gas emissions. To upscale whole-tree emissions, circumference at breast height (CBH) and height were measured.

CH4 Diffusion Rates (Diffusion_peepers.csv; Diffusion_sippers.csv)
To obtain porewater CH4 profiles (dc/dz), a porewater “sipper” was designed similar to commercial Rhizon samplers (Seeberg-Elverfeldt et al., 2005), but without the sampling biases. The sipper design is described in detail in Bridgham et al (2025). The design allows for 2 mL porewater samples to be taken over a 13 cm soil profile with a discrete zone of influence of < 0.5 cm (Seeberg-Elverfeldt et al., 2005). The sippers were placed into the peat 24 to 48 hr prior to sampling and each was sampled 1-3 times during the September 2018 and June 2019 campaigns. In the laboratory, gas samples collected from the sippers were injected into an SRI gas chromatograph equipped with flame ionization detector (Torrance, CA, USA), and total CH4 concentration in the headspace and porewater were calculated with Henry’s Law accounting for soil temperatures (Bridgham & Ye, 2013).
Additionally, more limited porewater sampling was conducted with diffusion-based “peepers” (Hesslein, 1976) to measure CO2 and CH4 concentrations and stable isotope ratios at 1 cm resolution near the surface of hollows inside SPRUCE enclosures. The peepers are comprised of a sheet of plexiglass with 8-mL grooves routed into the surface at 1 cm intervals. Prior to deployment, the routed grooves were filled with distilled water and covered with a polycarbonate membrane that is permeable to diffusing gas. The peepers were pressed into the peat surface to the desired depth and left to equilibrate for 4 weeks from July 2017 to August 2017. On retrieval, each section was sampled by inserting a needle attached to a syringe through the membrane, drawing up the porewater. Dissolved porewater CO2 and CH4 concentrations and isotopes were analyzed simultaneously via headspace analysis using a Finnigan Mat Delta V Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer coupled to a gas chromatograph (Merritt et al., 1995). The analytical uncertainty based on repeated measurements of a standard was <0.15 ‰ for δ13CO2 and δ13CH4 and <5 % for CO2 and CH4 concentrations. All isotope values are reported in δ notation relative to the PDB standard. Headspace concentrations were corrected using Henry’s Law to derive the total CO2 and CH4 in the headspace and water.
Diffusion rates (J) were estimated in the same plots used for the whole-plot CH4 emissions using Fick’s First Law of Diffusion:
J = O-DCH4 dc/dz,
where O is soil porosity (cm3 cm-3), DCH4 is the CH4 diffusion coefficient (cm2 sec-1), and dc/dz is the change in CH4 concentration with depth below the water table. A soil porosity of 0.88 was used, reflecting values measured by SPRUCE scientists at annual peat coring events. The pressure and temperature-corrected diffusion coefficient for CH4 in water was obtained from the formula in Riley & Skirrow (1975, p. 338) with DCH4 under standard conditions (25 °C, 1 atmosphere, 0 psu) obtained from Sahores et al. (1966).
